cue: The picture runs slowly, then jumps ahead to catch up.
rows: Birds can see a light flicker 40 to 140 times a second, and the fastest fliers are at the top of that range. People see flicker up to about 60 times a second. This view runs slowly and then jumps ahead to suggest the difference.
Most birds see half as much detail as people do, or less.
Some birds can see ultraviolet light, which people can’t. Phone cameras capture very little of it, so the violet tint in this view stands in for it.
Eyes on the sides of the head probably give a wide view. This part of the view is a guess.

src: research/birds drafts/birds.md L220: Hart 2001 (ultraviolet classes 360 to 373 nm in songbirds)
research/birds evidence L38 (oil droplets push the long class to about 610 nm)

spectrum.name: shift
spectrum.note: each class on one of the screen's three, the guessed ultraviolet in the bluest slot (atlas 5)

spectrum.name: wheel
spectrum.note: a finger dragged across the picture turns which three of the four classes are shown (atlas 5)

spectrum.name: neutral
spectrum.note: where the animal sees no colour and a person does, a faint shimmer like heat haze (atlas 4)

steady.name: lock
steady.note: the picture holds still in the world against the hand, then snaps to catch up (atlas 11)

steady.name: arm
steady.note: the picture moves only when the phone is jerked forward, as a pigeon thrusts its head
